problem:
Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

| ${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | $-3t$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} | $1-6t$ |  |  |
worked_solution:
We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ 12 & -4\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & -3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =8{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+6t) \\ 12{\alpha }_{1}t & =12{e}^{2t}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1+6t & -3t \\ 12t & 1-6t\end{aligned}].
$$
